cards.text: The word of the LORD comes to the prophet Ezekiel, and God calls him 'son of man.' His job is to take up a lament for Tyre, the city at the gateway to the sea, merchant to peoples on many coasts. But first, God repeats Tyre's own brag right back to it.

cards.question: What has Tyre been saying about itself?

answers.text: That it is perfect in beauty
That it can never be conquered
That it is older than every city

cards.text: Tyre's borders are in the heart of the seas, and its builders perfected its beauty. Me? I came out of a closing bakery's last bin with a 25 cent sticker on me. PERFECT was not on the sticker.
Then God describes the builders at work. All the planking is cypress from Senir, and they take a cedar from Lebanon to make the mast.

cards.question: With planking and a mast, God is picturing Tyre as a great ___.

cards.text: Oars of oak from Bashan, a deck of Cyprus wood inlaid with IVORY, and a sail of embroidered linen from Egypt. Friend, my bakery floor is inlaid with flour. Mostly by accident.

cards.question: Tyre's builders went cheap and used whatever wood was lying around.

cards.text: A ship this fancy needs a crew, and the men of Sidon and Arvad pull the oars.

cards.question: So who stands as captains of Tyre's ship?

cards.text: The elders of Gebal come aboard too. Their job? Shipwrights.

cards.question: Even Tyre's ship, perfect in beauty, has leaks that need repairing.

cards.text: Perfect in beauty, and it LEAKS, which I respect, because I had blurry edges for years. Then all the ships of the sea pull up alongside Tyre, sailors and all.

cards.question: Why do all the ships of the sea come alongside Tyre?

cards.text: Now the picture moves to Tyre's walls. Men of Persia, Lydia and Put serve as warriors in its army, and they hang their shields and helmets on those walls.

cards.question: The shields and helmets those warriors hang on Tyre's walls give it splendor.
Men of Arvad, Helech and Gammad guard Tyre's walls and towers, and their shields hung all around the walls ___ Tyre's beauty.

cards.text: Then comes a long list of Tyre's trading partners, nation after nation: silver, iron, tin and lead from Tarshish, wheat and honey from Judah and Israel, gold and spices from Sheba. Friend, I spent years under old receipts in a junk drawer, and not ONE of them was this long.
Business is BOOMING: the ships of Tarshish carry Tyre's merchandise, and Tyre is filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea. Then its oarsmen bring it out onto the high seas.

cards.question: Out on the high seas, what does God say will shatter Tyre?
When Tyre sinks into the heart of the sea, its riches go down, but everyone on board is spared.

cards.text: The countryside shakes when Tyre's sailors cry out. And all who handle the oars abandon their ships.

cards.question: After abandoning their ships, the sailors and all the captains of the sea stand on the ___.

cards.text: They raise their voices and cry out bitterly for Tyre. They throw dust on their heads and roll in ashes.

cards.question: Then the sailors shave their heads and wrap themselves in sackcloth. What are they showing?

cards.text: As they wail, the sailors take up a lament of their own, just like God told Ezekiel to take up. It opens: 'Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?'

cards.question: Looking back, the sailors say Tyre's abundant wealth and merchandise ___ the kings of the earth.

cards.text: But now Tyre is shattered by the seas in the depths of the waters, and its merchandise and people have gone down with it. Friend, I know what it's like to end up at the bottom of something, and mine was only a junk drawer.

cards.question: How do the people of the coastlands react to Tyre being shattered?

answers.text: They sail out to rebuild it

cards.question: The sailors' lament ends with hope that Tyre will one day rise again.

cards.text: Those who trade among the nations hiss at Tyre. Friend, that's the last sound in the whole lament, and it's not a song.

findings.problem: The blank tests 'perfected' from the repeated line in Ezekiel 27:11 ('they perfected your beauty'). That line first appears in 27:4 ('your builders perfected your beauty'), and card 3 already told it with the same word. The card asks about the repeat, and the baker can match the word from card 3 instead of reasoning it out.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers share one pattern ('Men hired from Persia', 'Men hired from Egypt'), and the right answer is the only one built differently ('Tyre's own men of skill'). The odd one out stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The question begins 'After abandoning their ships', which rules out the wrong answer 'deck'. Only 'shore' and 'walls' are left as real options.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: In the BSB, Ezekiel 27:26-36 is prophecy in the future tense ('will shatter', 'will sink', 'The countryside will shake', 'they will take up a lament'). Card 3 signals this ('what does God say will shatter Tyre'). From card 4 on, the cards tell it in the present tense as if it is happening ('When Tyre sinks', 'The countryside shakes', 'the sailors take up a lament'). A baker could come away thinking the passage reports Tyre's sinking as something that already happened, not something God says will happen.
findings.question: In prophetic passages, may Papa Dorin tell predicted future events in the present tense as storytelling? Or must the cards keep the text's future framing, such as 'will' or 'God says this is coming'?
